slides.title: Osteology of the lower limbs - Femur
slides.text:
Osteology of the lower limbs - Femur
The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body
Divided into proximal end, shaft and distal end
The proximal end features the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters
The shaft is also the body
The distal end features the medial and lateral condyles, and the epicondyles, as well as the patella surface

slides.title: Osteology of the lower limbs - Tibia
slides.text:
Osteology of the lower limbs - Tibia
Strong and weight-bearing bone of the lower limb
It has a proximal end, shaft and distal end
The proximal end features a top flat surface, called Tibial plateau for articulation with the condyles of the femur to form the knee joint
The upper-anterior surface at the proximal end features a roughened area called Tibial tuberosity for the attachment of the patella ligament

slides.title: Blood supply to the lower limbs
slides.text:
Blood supply to the lower limbs
The abdominal aorta at the level of the L4 bifurcates into right and left common iliac arteries
The external carotid artery (branch of common iliac artery) enters the pelvis running behind the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery
The femoral artery is the main supply to the lower limbs
It gives off the large profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery in the femoral triangle, which supplies the deep and posterior/medial muscles of the thigh

slides.title: The gluteal region
slides.text:
The gluteal region
The gluteal region (hip and buttocks) is the prominent area posterior to the pelvis
It is bounded superiorly by the iliac crest, greater trochanter, and ASIS and inferiorly by the gluteal fold
The gluteal fold also demarcates the superior boundary of the thigh
The intergluteal cleft separates the buttocks from each other

slides.title: The gluteal region
slides.text:
The gluteal region
Note that the parts of the bony pelvis—hip bones, sacrum, and coccyx—are held together by gluteal ligaments (sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments)
These  convert the sciatic notches in the hip bones into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
The greater sciatic foramen is the passageway for structures entering or leaving the pelvis
But the lesser sciatic foramen is a passageway for structures entering or leaving the perineum

slides.title: The gluteal muscles
slides.text:
The gluteal muscles
Has 2 layers: superficial and deep
superficial layer: consists of three large glutei (maximus, medius, and minimus) and the tensor fasciae latae
deep layer: consists of smaller muscles, the piriformis, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, and quadratus femoris
gluteus maximus: extension and lateral rotation of the thigh
Gluteus medius and minimus: abductors and medial rotators of the thigh
tensor fasciae latae is primarily a flexor of the thigh; acts in concert with the iliopsoas and rectus femoris
The deep muscles are lateral rotators of the thigh

slides.title: Gluteal region - Blood supply
slides.text:
Gluteal region - Blood supply
The arteries supplying this region are branches of the internal iliac artery
The major gluteal branches of the internal iliac artery are the superior and inferior gluteal arteries and the internal pudendal artery.
The superior and inferior gluteal arteries leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and pass superior and inferior to the piriformis, respectively
The internal pudendal artery enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen inferior to the piriformis and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen
Superior gluteal artery (SGA):
Superficial branch: gluteus maximus
Deep branch: gluteus medius and minimus and tensor fasciae latae
IGA: Gluteus maximus, obturator internus, quadratus femoris, and superior parts of hamstrings
IPA: External genitalia and muscles in the perineal region; does not supply gluteal region

slides.title: Joints of the Lower limb - The hip joint
slides.text:
Joints of the Lower limb - The hip joint
Ball and socket type of synovial joint
Formed by head of femur (the ball) and acetabulum of the hip bone (the socket)
The joint is held in place by the acetabular labrum which deepens the socket and helps grabs the femoral head
The transverse acetabular ligament is attached to the rim of the acetabulum and helps hold the joint

slides.title: The hip joint
slides.text:
The hip joint
A strong fibrous articular capsule attaches proximally to the acetabulum and transverse acetabular ligament, and distally to the neck of the femur
At its distal attachment, it is attached anteriorly to the intertrochanteric line and root of greater trochanter
And posteriorly, it runs over the intertrochanteric crest without being attached to it
Portions of the capsule thickens to form the hip joint ligaments: iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments
The ligament of the head of femur is attached to the margins of the acetabular notch, transverse acetabular ligament and pit in the head of femur
It also contains a small artery to the head of femur

slides.text:
The hip joint
Movements:
Flexion: iliopsoas, sartorius, tensor fascia lata, rectus femoris, pectineus, adductor longus and brevis, anterior part of adductor magnus, gracilis
Extension: Hamstrings (semi-tendinosus, semi-membranosus, long head of biceps femoris), posterior part of adductor magnus, gluteus maximus
Adduction: Gluteus medius and minimus, tensor fascia lata
Adduction: Adductor longus, Adductor brevis, Adductor magnus, gracilis, pectineus, obturator externus
Medial rotation: anterior fibres of gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensior fascia lata
Lateral rotation: obturator externus, obturator internus, gemelli, piriformis, quadratus femoris, gluteus maximus

slides.title: Knee joint
slides.text:
Knee joint
The knee joint is a hinge type of joint, formed by the articulation of three main bones
Femur: The distal end features medial and lateral condyles that articulate with the tibia
Tibia (Shinbone): The proximal end (tibial plateau) receives the femoral condyles
Patella (Kneecap): A sesamoid bone located within the quadriceps tendon that slides over the anterior surface of the distal femur (patellofemoral joint), increasing the leverage of the quadriceps muscle

slides.title: Ankle joint
slides.text:
Ankle joint
It is a hinge-type of synovial joint
Located between the distal ends of tibia and fibula and the superior parts of talus
Articular surfaces formed by;
the distal ends of the tibia and fibula
along with the inferior transverse part of the posterior tibiofibular ligament
This forms a malleolar mortise (deep socket)
Then the pulley-shaped trochlea of the talus fits into this mortise
The tibia articulates with the talus in two places:
Its inferior surface forms the roof of the malleolar mortise, transferring the body's weight to the talus
Its medial malleolus articulates with the medial surface of the talus
Note
The trochlea is the rounded superior articular surface of the talus
The medial surface of the lateral malleolus of fibula articulates with the lateral surface of the talus

slides.title: Ankle joint
slides.text:
Ankle joint
The malleoli grip the talus tightly as it rocks in the mortise during movements of the ankle joint
The grip of the malleoli on the trochlea is strongest during dorsiflexion of the foot
This movement forces the wider, anterior part of the trochlea posteriorly, spreading the tibia and fibula slightly apart
The ankle joint is relatively unstable during plantarflexion
This is because the trochlea is narrower posteriorly and therefore lies loosely within the mortise during plantarflexion

slides.title: Ankle joint
slides.text:
Ankle joint
Pott fracture-dislocation of the ankle
occurs when the foot is forcibly everted esp.in contact sports
This pulls on the medial ligament, and tearing off the medial malleolus
The talus moves laterally, shearing off the lateral malleolus also
or, more commonly, breaking the fibula superior to the tibiofibular syndesmosis
If the tibia is carried anteriorly, the posterior margin of the distal end of the tibia is also sheared off by the talus

slides.title: The Thigh
slides.text:
The Thigh
Made up of 3 compartments
Anterior Compartment (Extensors):
Quadriceps Femoris: Comprises the rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and vastus intermedius. They extend the knee and help flex the hip
Sartorius: A long, strap-like muscle that helps flex, abduct, and laterally rotate the hip, and flex the knee
Iliopsoas & Pectineus: Assist with hip and thigh flexion
Innervation: femoral nerve

slides.title: The Thigh
slides.text:
The Thigh
Medial Compartment (Adductors):
Comprises the adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, gracilis, and pectineus
Action: Adduction of the thigh and helps stabilize the pelvis
Innervation: Primarily supplied by the obturator nerve (with dual innervation from the sciatic nerve for part of the adductor magnus)
Posterior Compartment (Hamstrings):
Comprises the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus.
Action: flexes the knee and extends (straighten) the hip
Innervation:  Sciatic nerve (tibial and common fibular divisions)

slides.title: The Thigh – Femoral triangle
slides.text:
The Thigh – Femoral triangle
The femoral triangle is a wedge-shaped subfascial depression located at the upper third of the anterior thigh
It is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, medially by adductor longus and laterally by sartorius
Roof by deep fascia, floor by IPPA (iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus)
It is a passageway for nerves and vessels thus forming its contents: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal and deep inguinal lymph nodes

slides.title: The leg
slides.text:
The leg
Region between knee and ankle
The leg is divided into three tight fascial compartments
Anterior (Extensors/dorsiflexors)
Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius
Action: extends toes, dorsiflexes foot (to lift the foot upward)
Posterior (Flexors/Plantarflexors)
Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris
Lateral (Evertors)
Fibularis (peroneus) longus and fibularis brevis

slides.title: Popliteal fossa
slides.text:
Popliteal fossa
Diamond-shaped depression at back of knee and serves as passageway for neurovascular structures
Boundaries:
Superomedial: Semimembranosus and semitendinosus muscles
Superolateral: Biceps femoris muscle
Inferomedial: Medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle
Inferolateral: Lateral head of the gastrocnemius and the plantaris muscle
Floor (anterior wall): Popliteal surface of the femur, knee joint capsule, and popliteus muscle
Roof: Skin and popliteal fascia
Contents: sciatic nerve and its terminal branches (tibial and common peroneal), popliteal artery and vein, popliteal lymph nodes
Clinicals
Baker’s cyst: inflammation of semimembranosus bursa
Popliteal artery aneurysm
Popliteal lymphadenopathy

slides.title: The Foot
slides.text:
The Foot
Divided into 3 main regions
Hindfoot: Formed by the talus (ankle bone that connects to the tibia and fibula) and the calcaneus (heel bone)
Midfoot: formed by the navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiforms (medial, intermediate, and lateral)
Forefoot: Composed of five metatarsals (from big toe to little toe) and 14 phalanges
The muscle compartment is divided surgically into 3 by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa of the deep plantar fascia
Lateral, intermediate and medial compartments
For descriptive purposes, the muscle compartments is divided into four layers, from the plantar to the dorsal surface

slides.title: Arches of the Foot
slides.text:
Arches of the Foot
This is a skeletal framework that acts as a springboard for the foot
It transmits weight from the leg to the ground
It provides motion stability
It is formed by the tarsal bones, metatarsals and plantar ligaments
Transverse arch
anterior transverse arch (metatarsal bases/heads) and a posterior transverse arch (cuboid and cuneiforms)
Supported by the fibularis longus tendon and interosseous/plantar ligaments

slides.title: XRAY FILM STRUTURE
slides.text:
XRAY FILM STRUTURE
What is a radiographic film?
This is a special photographic film coated with a light sensitive emulsion containing silver halide crystals used to record and display xray image
A transparent base
Acts as detector, display and archive image in a single sheet
Still used in many departments even as digital systems replaces it
paragraphTexts: XRAY FILM STRUTURE

slides.title: Types of xray film
slides.text:
Types of xray film
Single sided emulsion film
Single-emulsion film has emulsion on one side of the polyester base.
Contain anti-curl or anti halation layer on the opposite side to keep the film flat
Single-emulsion systems can be selected where fine detail is prioritised.
Mostly used in mammography
Double sided emulsion film
Double-emulsion film has emulsion on both sides.
Double-emulsion film is common in screen-film radiography.

slides.title: Film base
slides.text:
Film base
Supports the emulsion layer and gives strength.
Usually made of polyester (polyethylene terephthalate, about 0.18 mm thick) in modern radiographic film, before it was cellulose triacetate
Polyester is usually tinted blue to reduce eye strain when viewing
Gives the film its rigidity so it can be handled and illuminated on a viewbox
N/B The base is only a support; it carries no image.

slides.title: Emulsion and gelatin
slides.text:
Emulsion and gelatin
Emulsion contains silver-halide crystals dispersed in gelatin.
Gelatin holds crystals evenly and permits processing chemicals to reach them.
The emulsion is the image-forming layer.
Scratches or chemical damage may affect processing process.

slides.title: Silver-halide crystals
slides.text:
Silver-halide crystals
They are light sensitive chemical compounds found in emulsion layer of the xray film
They are responsible for forming the latent image when exposed to light from intensifying screen or radiation
Usually contain silver bromide (AgBr), sometimes combined with smaller amount of other silver halides like silver chloride (AgCL) and silver iodide (AgI).
paragraphTexts: Silver-halide crystals

Usually contain silver bromide (AgBr), sometimes combined with smaller amount of other silver halides like silver chloride (AgCL) and silver iodide (AgI).

slides.title:
Latent image: from invisible to visible
(from invisible exposure to visible radiographic image)
slides.text:
Latent image: from invisible to visible
(from invisible exposure to visible radiographic image)
Summary of events that take place when emulsion is exposed to radiation
Exposure strikes the silver halide crystals producing an invisible chemical changes (latent image).
Developer reduces exposed crystals to black metallic silver forming radiographic image.
Fixer removes most unexposed silver halide crystals, leaving a permanent image made primarily of metallic silver.
Washing removes residual chemicals; drying prepares the film for viewing.

slides.title: The cassette and intensifying screens
slides.text:
The cassette and intensifying screens
Cassette holds film and excludes ambient light.
Intensifying screens convert X-ray energy into visible light.
Good film-screen contact reduces blur.
Intensifying screen cleanliness and cassette condition are part of quality assurance.

slides.title: Adhesive layer
slides.text:
Adhesive layer
Can as well be called compromise, substratum or subbing layer
This layer is made up of cellulose ester and gelatin in water and acetone, earlier made up of collodion.
Bonds emulsion to the base
Stays flexible when film is bent
Stops emulsion lifting in processing

slides.text:
SUPERCOAT
Hard, thin gelatin outer layer spread onto the surface of the emulsion
Protects against scratches and pressure, that is mechanical damage
Gives a shining surface for good appearance and durability

Used in selected applications, including some dental techniques.

slides.title: Developer: what it does
slides.text:
Developer: what it does
Reduces exposed silver-halide crystals to black metallic silver.
Affects film density and contrast(difference in density between between adjacent structures).
Time, temperature and chemical activity (strength) are important.
Depleted or incorrectly maintained developer can cause poor images and affect diagnosis.
paragraphTexts: Developer: what it does
Reduces exposed silver-halide crystals to black metallic silver.
Affects film density and contrast(difference in density between between adjacent structures).
Time, temperature and chemical activity (strength) are important.
Depleted or incorrectly maintained developer can cause poor images and affect diagnosis.

slides.title: RINSE,Fixer, washing and drying
slides.text:
RINSE,Fixer, washing and drying
Rinse remove residual developer chemical before fixing
Fixer removes unexposed silver halide.
Washing removes residual processing chemicals.
Poor washing may cause stains and poor archival stability.
Drying should avoid dust, excessive heat and physical damage.

slides.title: Safe film handling
slides.text:
Safe film handling
Avoid fingerprints, bending, pressure and scratches.
Keep film away from moisture, dust and chemicals.
Protect unexposed film from light and radiation.
Hold film by the edges with clean, dry hands
Load and unload only in the darkroom with the door closed
Slide film into the cassette gently to avoid scratches
Never touch screens with fingers or sharp objects

slides.title: Film storage
slides.text:
Film storage
Keep film in original packaging within manufacturer limits.
Protect film from heat (10–21 °C), relative humidity (40–60%), sunlight, chemical fumes and radiation.
Use first-expiry-first-out stock or first in first out (FIFO).
Film should be stored in boxes or carton in an upright position
Record batch numbers and expiry dates.

slides.title: Darkroom and safelight practice
slides.text:
Darkroom and safelight practice
Darkroom should be light-tight, clean and organised.
Use the correct safelight filter, wattage and distance.
Test for safelight fog when required.
Load and unload film only under approved conditions.
15-watt lamp and at least 1.2 m (4 ft) from the work bench
Keep wet and dry areas separate and the room clean and ventilated

slides.title: Spectral Sensitivity of Films
slides.text:
Spectral Sensitivity of Films
Is the ability of a film to respond to different wavelengths (colours) of light to form an image
It ensures that the film matches the colour of light emitted by the intensifying screen
It improves image formation and helps prevent unnecessary radiation exposure
It reduces film screen mismatch
paragraphTexts: Spectral Sensitivity of Films

slides.title: Classes of spectral sensitivity
slides.text:
Classes of spectral sensitivity
Blue-sensitive film (monochromatic film)
Responds mainly to blue and near-ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 380-495nm.
Used with compatible blue-emitting intensifying screens such as calcium tungstate
Safelight conditions must match the film specification.
Correct pairing supports efficient image formation

slides.title: INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER IN MEDICAL IMAGING
slides.text:
INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER IN MEDICAL IMAGING
A computer in radiography is an electronic device or system used to process, store, retrieve, display, and transmit radiographic images and patient information in a medical imaging department.
Computers play an important role in modern radiography, especially in digital X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), fluoroscopy, and other medical imaging techniques.
paragraphTexts: INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER IN MEDICAL IMAGING
A computer in radiography is an electronic device or system used to process, store, retrieve, display, and transmit radiographic images and patient information in a medical imaging department.
Computers play an important role in modern radiography, especially in digital X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), fluoroscopy, and other medical imaging techniques.

slides.title: Applications of Computers in Radiography
slides.text:
Applications of Computers in Radiography
IMAGE ACQUISITION
Computers receive digital image data from X-ray detectors and other imaging equipment.
IMAGE PROCESSING
They help adjust image brightness, contrast, sharpness, and magnification to improve image presentation
IMAGE STORAGE AND RETRIEVAL
Computers store images in systems such as PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) and allow them to be retrieved when needed.
PATIENT AND EXAMINATION MANAGEMENT
Computers manage patient records, examination requests, appointments, and radiology reports.
IMAGE DIAGNOSIS AND INTERPRETATION
They enable radiologists to examine images, perform measurements, and use specialized software to support diagnosis.
paragraphTexts: Applications of Computers in Radiography
IMAGE ACQUISITION
Computers receive digital image data from X-ray detectors and other imaging equipment.
IMAGE PROCESSING
They help adjust image brightness, contrast, sharpness, and magnification to improve image presentation
IMAGE STORAGE AND RETRIEVAL
Computers store images in systems such as PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) and allow them to be retrieved when needed.
PATIENT AND EXAMINATION MANAGEMENT
Computers manage patient records, examination requests, appointments, and radiology reports.
IMAGE DIAGNOSIS AND INTERPRETATION
They enable radiologists to examine images, perform measurements, and use specialized software to support diagnosis.

Storage devices: Hard disk drives (HDDs) and solid-state drives (SSDs) store images and information.

Computed Radiography (CR) systems: Use imaging plates that are read by a reader to produce digital images.
Digital Radiography (DR) systems: Use digital detectors to capture X-ray images directly.
CT computer systems: Process data collected from multiple X-ray projections to reconstruct cross-sectional images.
MRI computer systems: Process signals from the body to produce detailed images.
PACS: Stores, retrieves, distributes, and displays medical images.
RIS (Radiology Information System): Manages radiology workflow, examinations, patient information, and reporting.

slides.title: Data and Information in Radiography
slides.text:
Data and Information in Radiography
Data are raw facts, figures, observations, or measurements collected during a radiographic examination before they have been processed or interpreted into meaningful information.
Examples of data in radiography include:
Patient's age and identification number.
Patient's weight and height.
Exposure factors such as kVp, mA, and exposure time.
X-ray detector readings.
Raw digital image values.

slides.title: Definition of Information
slides.text:
Definition of Information
Information is data that have been processed, organized, or interpreted to give meaningful results that can be used for decision-making.
Examples of information in radiography include:
A patient's completed radiographic report.
A calculated exposure time based on selected parameters.
A processed chest X-ray image displayed on a monitor.
A report describing a fracture identified on an X-ray.

slides.title: Types of Data in Radiography
slides.text:
Types of Data in Radiography
Patient data: Name, age, sex, identification number, and medical history.
Examination data: Type of examination, anatomical region, projection, and date of examination.
Technical data: kVp, mA, exposure time, mAs, source-to-image distance (SID), and focal spot size.
Image data: Pixel values, image dimensions, brightness values, and contrast information.
Diagnostic data: Findings documented by the radiologist, such as fractures, lung opacities, or joint abnormalities.

slides.title: How Data Becomes Information in Radiography
slides.text:
How Data Becomes Information in Radiography
Data collection
Patient details, exposure factors and detector signals
Data processing
Computer processing, image reconstruction and enhancement
Information output
Displayed radiographic image and organized examination details
Interpretation and decision-making
Radiologist interprets the image and prepares a report
For example, a digital detector collects numerical signals during an X-ray exposure. The imaging computer processes these signals to form an image. The radiologist then interprets the image and produces a diagnostic report.

Word processing is the use of computer software to create, edit, format, save, print, and share text documents.
In radiography, word processing is used to prepare radiographic reports, patient records, referral letters, departmental memos, research papers, and other medical documents.
Examples of word-processing software include Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and LibreOffice Writer.

The internet is a worldwide network of interconnected computers and devices that communicate and exchange information electronically.
In radiography, the internet allows radiographers, radiologists, and other healthcare professionals to access medical information, share radiographic images, communicate with colleagues, and participate in online learning.

In radiography, digital communication is used to transfer radiographic images, patient examination details, and diagnostic reports between healthcare professionals and medical facilities.

slides.title: A daylight film processor is a radiographic film processing system that allows radiographers to handle and process X-ray films in normal room light without using a darkroom.
slides.text:
A daylight film processor is a radiographic film processing system that allows radiographers to handle and process X-ray films in normal room light without using a darkroom.
It uses a special light-tight system to protect the unexposed film from unwanted light while the film is being loaded, processed, and removed.
CONCEPT OF DAYLIGHT FILM PROCESSING
paragraphTexts: A daylight film processor is a radiographic film processing system that allows radiographers to handle and process X-ray films in normal room light without using a darkroom.
It uses a special light-tight system to protect the unexposed film from unwanted light while the film is being loaded, processed, and removed.
CONCEPT OF DAYLIGHT FILM PROCESSING

slides.title: The process generally follows these steps:
slides.text:
The process generally follows these steps:
1. Film loading
The exposed X-ray cassette is placed into the daylight loading compartment.
Film extraction
The system opens the cassette inside a light-protected compartment and removes the exposed film.
Film processing
The film passes through the processing stages: developing, fixing, washing, and drying. Some systems integrate these stages into an automatic processor.
Film collection
The processed, dry radiograph is delivered for viewing and interpretation.
MODE OF OPERATION

slides.title: The main components may include:
slides.text:
The main components may include:
Film loading compartment — receives the exposed cassette.
Cassette opening mechanism — opens the cassette safely within the protected chamber.
Film extraction mechanism — removes the film from the cassette.
Light-tight chamber — prevents unwanted light from reaching the film.
Film transport system — moves the film through the processor.
Processing unit — carries out developing, fixing, washing, and drying.
Film collection tray — receives the finished radiograph.

The concept of digital X-ray processing is the acquisition of X-ray information by a digital detector, conversion of the information into numerical data, computer processing of the data to form an image, and subsequent display, storage and transmission of that image for diagnostic purposes.
Unlike conventional film-screen radiography, which uses photographic film and chemical processing, digital radiography uses electronic detectors and computer technology to produce images.
BASIC PRINCIPLES OF DIGITAL IMAGING
paragraphTexts: The concept of digital X-ray processing is the acquisition of X-ray information by a digital detector, conversion of the information into numerical data, computer processing of the data to form an image, and subsequent display, storage and transmission of that image for diagnostic purposes.
Unlike conventional film-screen radiography, which uses photographic film and chemical processing, digital radiography uses electronic detectors and computer technology to produce images.

slides.title: Indirect-conversion DR: Uses a scintillator to convert X-rays into visible light, a photodiode array to convert light into electrical signals, and a TFT array to read out the signals.
slides.text:
Indirect-conversion DR: Uses a scintillator to convert X-rays into visible light, a photodiode array to convert light into electrical signals, and a TFT array to read out the signals.
Direct-conversion DR: Uses a direct-conversion material, such as amorphous selenium (a-Se), to convert X-rays directly into electrical charges. It does not require a scintillator or photodiode layer.
Important distinction: Computed radiography (CR) typically uses a photostimulable phosphor imaging plate, which stores a latent image that is later read by a laser scanner. The scintillator–photodiode–TFT arrangement describes an indirect-conversion flat-panel DR detector, rather than a typical CR imaging plate.
TYPES OF DR IMAGE FORMATION
paragraphTexts: Indirect-conversion DR: Uses a scintillator to convert X-rays into visible light, a photodiode array to convert light into electrical signals, and a TFT array to read out the signals.
Direct-conversion DR: Uses a direct-conversion material, such as amorphous selenium (a-Se), to convert X-rays directly into electrical charges. It does not require a scintillator or photodiode layer.

Important distinction: Computed radiography (CR) typically uses a photostimulable phosphor imaging plate, which stores a latent image that is later read by a laser scanner. The scintillator–photodiode–TFT arrangement describes an indirect-conversion flat-panel DR detector, rather than a typical CR imaging plate.

slides.title: 1. High initial cost: Digital X-ray equipment, computers, software, and detectors are expensive to purchase and install.
slides.text:
1. High initial cost: Digital X-ray equipment, computers, software, and detectors are expensive to purchase and install.
2. High maintenance cost: The equipment requires regular servicing, repairs, and software updates.
3. Dependence on electricity: Digital radiography systems require a reliable power supply to operate.
4. Risk of radiation overexposure: Image processing can make overexposed images appear acceptable, potentially encouraging unnecessary repeat exposures or gradual increases in patient dose (dose creep).
5. Technical failures: Detector malfunction, computer breakdown, or software errors can interrupt imaging services.
6. Need for trained personnel: Radiographers require appropriate training to operate the equipment and process images correctly.
Main disadvantages

8. Data storage requirements: Digital images require substantial storage capacity and reliable backup systems.
9. Cybersecurity and privacy risks: Patient images and records may be lost, accessed without authorization, or affected by cyberattacks.
10. Network problems: Slow networks or system failures can delay image transfer and reporting.
11. Equipment obsolescence: Rapid technological changes may make older systems outdated and expensive to upgrade.
12. Loss of image data: Accidental deletion, hardware failure, or inadequate backup can result in permanent loss of patient images.

slides.title: Power enters the generator: The mains electricity supplies the X-ray system.
slides.text:
Power enters the generator: The mains electricity supplies the X-ray system.
Exposure factors are selected: The radiographer chooses the appropriate kVp, mA and exposure time.
The filament is heated: The filament transformer supplies current to heat the cathode filament, releasing electrons.
High voltage is applied: The high-voltage circuit accelerates electrons across the vacuum inside the X-ray tube.
Electrons strike the anode: Their kinetic energy is converted mainly into heat, with a small fraction converted into X-rays.
The exposure stops: The timer or exposure-control circuit terminates the exposure at the required time.

Single-phase generator
Uses single-phase AC and produces greater voltage ripple than modern high-frequency systems.
Three-phase generator - 6 valves
Provides a more constant tube voltage and generally more efficient X-ray production than a single-phase generator.
Three-phase generator -12 valves
Supply high voltage to the X-ray tube with reduced voltage ripple, producing a more consistent X-ray beam and greater X-ray output efficiency than a single-phase generator under comparable conditions.
High-frequency generator
Uses electronic switching to produce a nearly constant tube voltage, allowing efficient operation and consistent exposures.
Constant potential generator: Keeps the selected (kVp) nearly constant throughout the exposure thereby Minimizes fluctuations in the voltage supplied to the X-ray tube.

X rays are produced when  high speed electrons emitted from the cathode filament are converted to x ray photons as they strike and interact with the target material. This process involved the following steps:-
Heated filament at the cathode         emission of electrons  to saturation points
Fast movement of electron  due to high potential difference across vacuum x ray tube.
Bombardment of target surface  at anode interaction of anode target  material by fast moving electrons.
Deceleration of electrons and subsequent loss of energy of electron to release x ray photons.

slides.title: There are two methods of X ray production
slides.text:
There are two methods of X ray production
Continuous Spectrum (Bremsstrahlung or breaking radiation):- In this process the fast moving electron interact with the target atom and are deflected from their original direction or path thereby loss energy and are decelerated. The kinetic energy loss by the electron is emitted in form of a photon energy called x ray photons. This account for most x rays used in diagnosis
Characteristic radiation:- Is produced when the fast moving electron from the cathode filament interact and eject an inner electron from the orbit of the atom of the target material (Tungsten) thereby causing a vacant orbital shell within the atom of the target material and this vacant orbital shell will  cause electron transition from the outer shell to filled  the gap.

ANTI SCATTERED GRID
This is a device place between the patient and the image receptor to absorbed scattered radiation from getting to the receptor while allowing the primary x ray beam  that traverse the patient to reach the detector. It comprise of a thin strip of lead separated by some interspace radio parent   materials mostly made of organic compound or aluminum. It operates on the principle that scattered radiation are moving perpendicular to the direction of  primary beam and  are absorbed  by the lead strip
Grid ratio is a statement of the height of the lead strip to the distance of the interspace materials. This tells more of the efficacy of the grid. There are different types of grid
Linear grid: The lead strip are parallel to each other in their longitudinal axis.

slides.title: BUCKY  ASSEMBLY
slides.text:
BUCKY  ASSEMBLY
The movement of grid during exposure is aim at removing the grid lines from the image.
The main components are :- Grid moving mechanism, grid drive mechanism, detector holding tray, Bucky housing and grid
The Bucky assembly has its circuit that its energized during prep for exposure and this enable the grid to move until exposure is terminated.
There  are two types: Vertical and horizontal or table Bucky.
FUNCTIONS OF GRID
Reduces scattered radiation from the patients reaching the image receptor
Improves image contrast
Improves image quality
Reduces background fog
Improves diagnostic accuracy and visibility of thick body parts
Its also important to note that grid increases patient radiation dose due to increase in exposure factors.

Processing tanks:  Compartments holding temperature – controlled solutions for developing , fixing , and washing:
Developer Tank:  converts exposed silver halide crystals into black metallic silver ( typically maintained around 33 C / 96 F ).
Fixer Tank : Dissolves unexposed / underdeveloped silver halide and hardens the gelatin emulsion.
Wash Tank: Uses circulating water to flush away residual processing chemicals.
Recirculation and filtration system: continuously agitates, mixes ,  filters , and maintains even temperatures across the chemical baths.

slides.title: 1. PRINCIPLES OF AUTOMATIC PROCESSING:
slides.text:
1. PRINCIPLES OF AUTOMATIC PROCESSING:
The core principle of automatic processing is standardization of time , temperature , and chemical activity. It operates on the same chemical sequence as manual processing – developing, fixing , washing, and drying – but compresses the entire timeline ( typically down to 90 seconds ) by utilizing:
High chemical concentration:  Formulated specifically to handle aggressive development speed.
Elevated temperature:  Processing solution are heated to maximize chemical activity.

slides.title: Continuous mechanical agitation:  Constant contact between the rollers and the film emulsion forces fresh chemicals into the film surface while squeezing out exhausted solutions.

2. CONSTRUCTION AND DESIGN MECHANISM:
The processor consists of several independent but integrated sub-system:
Transport system:  A network of gears, chains, a drive motor, and precision roller racks designed to pull the film along a serpentine path through the liquid tanks and the drying chamber at a fixed speed.

slides.title: 3. FEED TRAY AND FEEDTRAY TYPES
slides.text:
3. FEED TRAY AND FEEDTRAY TYPES
The feed tray is the entry platform where the exposed radiographic film is introduced into the unit.
Mechanism:  It contains micro switches or infrared optical sensors that detect the physical presence, size ,and orientation of the inserted film. This detection signal activates the drive motor , the dryer, and calculates the required volume of replenisher chemicals.
paragraphTexts: 3. FEED TRAY AND FEEDTRAY TYPES
The feed tray is the entry platform where the exposed radiographic film is introduced into the unit.

Mechanism:  It contains micro switches or infrared optical sensors that detect the physical presence, size ,and orientation of the inserted film. This detection signal activates the drive motor , the dryer, and calculates the required volume of replenisher chemicals.

slides.title: Feed tray types:
slides.text:
Feed tray types:
Darkroom feed tray:  A standard tray located completely inside a darkroom under safelight condition where the operator manually feeds exposed films extracted from cassettes.
Daylight loader ( daylight feed tray ) :  A light – tight, enclosed chamber attachment fitted with sleeves or an automated cassette – unloading mechanism. This setup allows the operator to insert their hands and feed the film in normal room light without exposing the film emulsion.

slides.title: 4. ROLLERS ( TRANSPORT COMPONENTS )
slides.text:
4. ROLLERS ( TRANSPORT COMPONENTS )
The mechanical movement relies heavily on specialized rollers clustered into functional racks:
Entrance Rollers:  Located immediately past the feed tray, they grab the film and trigger the processing cycle.
Transport / Deep- Tank Rollers:  Positioned inside the liquid tanks, these planetary rollers guide the film downward and upward along the rack assembly.
paragraphTexts: 4. ROLLERS ( TRANSPORT COMPONENTS )
The mechanical movement relies heavily on specialized rollers clustered into functional racks:
Entrance Rollers:  Located immediately past the feed tray, they grab the film and trigger the processing cycle.
Transport / Deep- Tank Rollers:  Positioned inside the liquid tanks, these planetary rollers guide the film downward and upward along the rack assembly.

slides.title: Cross- over Rollers:  Situated above the solution levels between adjacent tanks ( e.g., developer to fixer). They feature miniature guide shoes to redirect the film from one path to the next.
slides.text:
Cross- over Rollers:  Situated above the solution levels between adjacent tanks ( e.g., developer to fixer). They feature miniature guide shoes to redirect the film from one path to the next.
Squeegee Rollers:  Located at the exit of the wash tank. They apply physical pressure to strip excess water from both sides of the film emulsion before it enters the drying chamber, reducing the energy needed for thermal drying.

slides.title: 5. REPLENISHMENT SYSTEM
slides.text:
5. REPLENISHMENT SYSTEM
As films pass through the chemistry ,solutions wear out ( developer oxidizes and loses electron. Fixers accumulates silver ions and dilutes ). The replenishment system injects exact doses of fresh chemicals from storage reservoirs into the active processor tanks to maintain stable chemical potency.
Volume ( pulse ) replenishment :  Triggered dynamically  whenever a film crosses the entry sensors . The pump inject a specified amount based on the length or surface area of the processed film.

slides.title: Flood ( timed ) Replenishment:   Configured for low- volume clinics . The processor automatically pulses fresh chemistry at a fixed time interval ( regardless of film throughout ) the combat natural aerial  oxidation.

Because automatic processing occurs at high speed and elevated temperatures , standard manual chemistry cannot be used. The chemistry must contain specialized hardening compounds to protect the film from swelling or melting.

Check the chemical volumes in the external replenishment tanks

slides.title: Why processing matters
slides.text:
Why processing matters
1. X-ray exposure: Photons strike the film emulsion
2. Latent image: Invisible change in silver halide
3. Processing: Chemistry reveals the image  and fixes it
4. Visible image: Metallic silver forms the radiograph
5. Diagnosis: Quality decides diagnostic value
Faulty processing can ruin a perfect exposure, causing repeats and extra dose.

slides.title: What is a single-bath system?
slides.text:
What is a single-bath system?
One solution performs developing and fixing in a single step (a monobath)
Developer and fixer chemicals are balanced to coexist in one tank
Development starts first; fixing then clears unexposed silver halide
Key point: One tank, one solution, one timed immersion.

slides.title: Chemistry inside a monobath
slides.text:
Chemistry inside a monobath
A developing agent and an alkali give the solution its developing power
A silver halide solvent (such as thiosulfate) gives it fixing power
The two actions are balanced, so no one is stronger than the other
Timing and temperature must follow the maker's instructions closely
Key point: A monobath is a chemical compromise: two jobs, one solution.

slides.title: How a monobath works
slides.text:
How a monobath works
1. Immerse: Film enters the single solution
2. Develop: Exposed crystals reduce to silver
3. Fix: Unexposed halide dissolves
4. Wash: Residual chemicals removed
5. Dry: Film hung to dry

slides.title: Problems with single-bath processing
slides.text:
Problems with single-bath processing
Weak contrast and low density compared with standard processing
Fogging if the bath is too warm
Short bath life, so results drift quickly
Residual silver compounds may remain and stain the film
Key point: Quality control is hard when one bath does everything.

slides.title: What is conventional processing?
slides.text:
What is conventional processing?
Developer, rinse, fixer and wash as separate solutions in separate tanks
The film moves from tank to tank on a hanger
Each stage mostly developing stage is controlled by time and temperature
It is the standard method of manual processing for diagnostic films
Key point: Separate baths, each doing one job well.

1. Developer tank: Makes the latent image visible
2. Rinse tank: Stops development
3. Fixer tank: Clears and fixes the image
4. Wash tank: Running water removes chemicals
5. Drying: Warm, filtered air
Tanks are arranged in the order the film travels.

slides.title: Manual processing technique
slides.text:
Manual processing technique
Clip the film by its corners on a clean, dry hanger
Lower it smoothly into the developer and start the timer
Agitate at the start and tap to release air bells
Drain, rinse, then fix for the full time
Wash in running water and dry without touching the surface
Key point: Smooth, timed, clean handling prevents most artifacts.

slides.title: Time and temperature control
slides.text:
Time and temperature control
Standard development is about 5 minutes at 20 °C
A warmer bath works faster and may fog the film
A cooler bath works slowly and under-develops
Use a thermometer and a timer for every film
Key point: Time and temperature must always be read together.

Tank arrangement
Tanks sit in a line: developer, rinse, fixer, wash
Film never travels back over a tank it has left
Each tank has its own lid and stirring rod
Wash tank sits last, with running water
Key point: A one-way path protects each solution from contamination.

Separation: Keep apart wet and dry bench so that water cannot reach the film
Dry bench: where cassettes are unloaded and loaded with new film.
Its top should be large enough to accommodate the biggest cassette.
The surface of the dry bench should be made up of either wood or linoleum
Wet bench: this is an area of processing unit where processing are carried out
Contain tanks, sink and wash facilities

CUPBOARDS: to stock recent film supply intended for replenishment of the film hopper. The cupboard dimension should allow film boxes to stand upright to avoid any form of static discharge

4. Descale: Remove deposits if present

slides.title: COR: Control of Chemistry and Replenishment
slides.text:
COR: Control of Chemistry and Replenishment
Why control processing?
Consistent density and contrast on every film
Fewer repeat and lower patient dose
Chemistry degrades with use, time and air
As a result there is need for replenisher to restores both chemistry and level
Four variables to control: time, temperature, concentration, purity
Key point: Controlled processing protects the image and the patient from radiation.

Developing agents: reduces exposed halide. Examples are Phenidone, hydroquinone, metol (elon), ascorbic acid and glycin

Restrainer: Potassium bromide limits fog
Preservative: Sulfite slows oxidation
Hardener: Limits gelatin swelling

Handling artifacts
Crescent marks: Cause: Film bent or kinked. Prevention: Hold by edges, avoid flexing
Finger marks: Cause: Dirty or wet hands. Prevention: Dry, clean hands
Static: Cause: Dry air, quick film removal. Prevention: Humidity control, slow handling
Scratches: Cause: Rough surfaces or hangers. Prevention: Smooth surfaces, careful loading

slides.title: Light and fog artifacts
slides.text:

Light fog: Cause: Light leak or white light. Prevention: Test and seal darkroom
Safelight fog: Cause: Wrong filter, bulb or distance. Prevention: Correct filter, 15 W, about 1.2 m
Chemical fog: Cause: Warm or contaminated developer. Prevention: Control temperature, fresh chemicals
Dichroic fog: Cause: Fixer in developer, weak fixing. Prevention: Prevent splashes, fresh fixer

Dark spots: Cause: Developer splashes before immersion. Prevention: Keep area clean
White spots: Cause: Fixer splashes before development. Prevention: Keep area clean

slides.title: How to Prevent artifacts
slides.text:
How to Prevent artifacts
Handle film by the edges with clean, dry hands
Keep solutions fresh, clean and at the right temperature
Agitate at the start of development and fixing
Wash thoroughly and dry in clean air
Study every artifact film, not only discard it
Key point: Every artifact points to the cause that should be fixed.

slides.title: Sequence of Processing
slides.text:
Sequence of Processing
The five stages
1. Develop: About 5 min at 20 °C
2. Rinse: About 30 to 60 seconds
3. Fix: About 10 minutes
4. Wash: 20 to 30 minutes
5. Dry: Warm filtered air
Each stage prepares the film for the next, and none can be skipped.

Check developer temperature and set the timer

Clip film firmly on the correct hanger
Hold hanger by the corners and edges only

slides.title: Processing stages
slides.text:
Processing stages
Stage 1: Developing
About 5 minutes at 20 °C, or as per the maker's chart
Agitate at the start, then at intervals
Exposed silver halide is reduced to metallic silver
Tap hanger to dislodge air bells
Drain for a few seconds before the rinse
Key point: The latent image becomes visible.
paragraphTexts: Processing stages
Stage 1: Developing
About 5 minutes at 20 °C, or as per the maker's chart
Agitate at the start, then at intervals
Exposed silver halide is reduced to metallic silver
Tap hanger to dislodge air bells
Drain for a few seconds before the rinse
Key point: The latent image becomes visible.

slides.title: Stage 2: Rinse (stop bath)
slides.text:
Stage 2: Rinse (stop bath)
30 to 60 seconds in agitated clean water or stop bath
Halts development and removes alkaline developer
Protects the fixer from rapid exhaustion
Drain before moving to the fixer
Key point: A good rinse protects the fixer and prevents stain.
paragraphTexts: Stage 2: Rinse (stop bath)
30 to 60 seconds in agitated clean water or stop bath
Halts development and removes alkaline developer
Protects the fixer from rapid exhaustion
Drain before moving to the fixer
Key point: A good rinse protects the fixer and prevents stain.

slides.title: Stage 3: Fixing
slides.text:
Stage 3: Fixing
About 10 minutes, at least twice the clearing time
Thiosulfate dissolves unexposed silver halide
Acid stops development and hardener firms the gelatin
Agitate on entry for even action
Check clearing time regularly
Key point: Fixing makes the image permanent and stable.
paragraphTexts: Stage 3: Fixing
About 10 minutes, at least twice the clearing time
Thiosulfate dissolves unexposed silver halide
Acid stops development and hardener firms the gelatin
Agitate on entry for even action
Check clearing time regularly
Key point: Fixing makes the image permanent and stable.

slides.title: Stage 4: Washing
slides.text:
Stage 4: Washing
20 to 30 minutes in running water
Removes residual thiosulfate and silver compounds
Poor washing causes brown stain with time
Key point: An incomplete wash shortens the life of the radiograph.
paragraphTexts: Stage 4: Washing
20 to 30 minutes in running water
Removes residual thiosulfate and silver compounds
Poor washing causes brown stain with time
Key point: An incomplete wash shortens the life of the radiograph.

slides.title: Stage 5: Drying
slides.text:
Stage 5: Drying
Warm, filtered air in a cabinet or rack
Dust and drips cause marks, so keep air clean
Wet film is soft and scratches easily
Remove from hangers only when completely dry
Label and file once dry
Key point: Handle wet film gently; the gelatin is soft.

slides.title: Silver Recovery and Conservation
slides.text:
Silver Recovery and Conservation
Silver recovery and conservation involve reclaiming precious metallic silver from used or discarded xray films.
Why recover silver?
Used fixer carries dissolved silver from unexposed halide
Silver has real economic value
Silver is toxic to aquatic life, so it must not go down drains
Regulations often require recovery or safe disposal
Key point:. Reduce repeats with correct exposure technique is essential for silver conservation

slides.title: Sources of silver
slides.text:
Sources of silver
Used fixer: Main source of dissolved silver
Fixer overflow: Carries silver out of the tank
Waste film: Rejected and old films contain silver
Wash water: Trace silver from carryover
paragraphTexts: Sources of silver
Used fixer: Main source of dissolved silver
Fixer overflow: Carries silver out of the tank

slides.title: Silver recovery methods
slides.text:
Silver recovery methods
Metallic replacement: Principle: Used fixer is passed through a container containing iron or steel wool.Steel wool or iron replaces silver from solution due to displacement action causing metallic silver to be deposited. Notes: Cheap, simple
Electrolytic: Principle: electric current is passed through used fixer solution. The current plates or collect silver onto a cathode. Notes: High recovery; fixer can often be reused
Chemical precipitation: Principle: Reagent or chemical added to the used fixer solution forms insoluble silver compound that can be separated and collected. Notes: Sludge (solid deposit containing recovered silver and other materials) needs careful handling
Ion exchange: Principle: Resin captures silver ions. Notes: Used on larger scales

Chemical precipitation: Principle: Reagent or chemical added to the used fixer solution forms insoluble silver compound that can be separated and collected. Notes: Sludge (solid deposit containing recovered silver and other materials) needs careful handling
Ion exchange: Principle: Resin captures silver ions. Notes: Used on larger scales

slides.title: Safe storage and disposal
slides.text:
Safe storage and disposal
Collect used fixer in labelled, sealed containers
Store away from developer, acids and heat
Use a licensed contractor to collect waste
Never pour used fixer or silver sludge down a drain
Keep disposal records for inspection
Key point: Recover, store safely, and dispose through approved routes.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.text:
Conclusion
Single-bath processing is simple but limited, and mainly a teaching concept
Conventional processing uses separate baths and gives reliable diagnostic quality
Always read time and temperature together
Keep developer and fixer apart at all times
Wash fully and dry in clean air
Recover silver and dispose of waste through approved routes

A) FORCE

fundamental forces: the strong nuclear force, (holding quarks and nucleons together) the weak nuclear force (responsibility responsible for radioactive decay like beta decay), the electromagnetic force (binding electrons to atomic nuclei), and gravity (negligible at the subatomic scale).

Definition: the spontaneous transfer of Thermal energy from a region or object of higher temperature. PROTONS:
CHARGE:  POSITIVE (+1}
Mass: Approximately 1 atomic mass unit {amu}
Role: The number of protons is the atomic number (Z). Which defines the identity of the chemical element (e.g, carbon always has 6 protons).
NEUTRONS:
CHARGE: Neutral (0, no charge)
Mass: Approximately 1 amu (very close to a protons mass)
Role:  They act as nuclear “glue “using the strong nuclear force to bind protons together and overcome electromagnetic repulsion.  Variants of an element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.

slides.title: Key features of the periodic table:
slides.text:
Key features of the periodic table:
Total elements: 118 confirmed chemical elements, ordered by increasing atomic number (number of protons) from Hydrogen ( 1) to organesson ( 118 ).
Periods (rows): There are 7 horizontal rows. Each period indicates the number of electron shells an atom has.
Groups (Columns): There are 18 vertical columns. Elements in the same group share similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.
Main classification:
Metals: Found on the left and center.

slides.title: 1. ISOTOPES ( changes in the nucleus )
slides.text:
1. ISOTOPES ( changes in the nucleus )
Isotopes are variants of a single chemical element that have same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in their nuclei.
The core concept: Because they have the same number of protons ( and electrons 0, isotopes of an element share the exact same chemical properties. However, because their neutrons counts differ, they have different physical masses.
Example: carbon – 12 and carbon – 14 are both isotopes of carbon. Both have 6 protons. Carbon – 12 has 6 neutrons ( stable and common ), while carbon – 14 has 8 neutrons ( unstable and radioactive, used in carbon dating ).

slides.title: IONIZATION ( loss or gain of electron )
slides.text:
IONIZATION ( loss or gain of electron )
Ionization is the process by which an atom or molecule gains a net positive or negative charge by gaining or losing electrons.
The core concept: Atoms are naturally neutral because they have an equal number of protons ( + ) and electrons ( - ) . If you add enough energy to an atom, you can completely rip an electron away from it. This  turns the neutral atom into a charged particle called an ion
Example. When a neutral sodium ( Na ) atom loses an electron, it becomes a positively charged sodium ion ( Na+ ).

slides.title: 3  EXCITATION ( Shifting Electron Energy Levels )
slides.text:
3  EXCITATION ( Shifting Electron Energy Levels )
Excitation occurs when an electron inside an atom absorbs energy and jump to a higher energy level ( shell ),without leaving the atom entirely,
The core concept: Unlike ionization – where the electron is permanently kicked out – excitation keeps the electron bound to the atom. The atom simply enters a temporary unstable “  excited state “”. When the electron eventually falls back down to its original, stable “ground state “, it releases that absorbed energy as a flash of light ( a photon ).
Example: Neon sign work because of excitation. Electricity pumps energy into the neon gas atoms, exiting their electrons. As those electrons drop back down to their normal level, they emit the glowing colored light you see.

ELECTRICAL CHARGE:
DEFINITION: Electrical charge is a functional physical property of subatomic particles  ( such as a  protons neutrons) that causes them to experience a force when placed in an electric or magnetic field. It is measured in coulombs ( C ).
Key Rules : Like charges repel each other, and opposite charges attract each othe. Charge is conserved and quantized.
Example: Rubbing a plastic comb against your hair transfers  electrons, giving the comb a negative electric charge that can pick up small pieces of paper.
ELECTRIC CURRENT:
Definition: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric chargepast a giving point in a circuit. It is measured in Amperes ( A ), where 1A = 1 c/s.
Key Rules: current  flows through a closed circuit from a higher potential ( Positive terminal ) to a low potential ( Negative terminal )

slides.title: Ohm”s Law
slides.text:
Ohm”s Law
Definition: A fundamental principle stating that the voltage  ( V ) across a conductor is directly proportional to the current ( I ) flowing through it, multiplied by the resistance:
Formula:   V = I * R  .( Also written as I = V/R or R = V/I )
Example: If you connect a 12 – volt battry ( V = 12V ) to a circuit with a 4 ohm”s resistance ( R = 4ohm”s ) the current ( I ) flowing through the circuit will be I = 12V/ 4 ohm”S = 3amps.
To calculate total resistance ( Rtotal ) , use simple algebraic formulas depending on whether the component are wired in a series or parallel configuration.

slides.title: 1. Resistance in series
slides.text:
1. Resistance in series
Rules: current flows sequentially through a single path. So you add the individual resistance values together.
Formula: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + …..; example: you have three resistors in series with the following values: R1 = 100 ohm””s , R2 = 20 ohm”s ,and R3 = 30 ohm”s.
Rtotal =( 100 + 20 + 30 ) ohm””s  = 150 ohm”s
Key takeaway: The total resistance in series is always greater than the largest individual resistance

POWER
Definition: power is the rate at which energy is transferred, used, or converted over time.
SI unit: Watt ( W ) , which equals one joule per second ( J/S }.
Fomula: Power = Energy / time (  P = W/ t }.
Key concept : Power tells you how fast energy is being used or delivered , not just the total amount.
Examole:
Light bulb: A 60 – watt light bulb uses 60 joules of electrical energy every single second.
Appliances: A 1.500 – watt microwave cooks food much faster than a lower – powered device because it transfers energy at a higher rate
Human/ Mechanic Work:  A weightlifter lifting a heavy barbell quickly exerts more power than some one lifting the same weight very slowly.

slides.title: THE HEATING EFFECTS OF A CURRENT.
slides.text:
THE HEATING EFFECTS OF A CURRENT.
The heating effect of an electric current – also known as joule heating or resistive heating – occurs when an electric current flows through a conductor and encounters resistance. As free electrons move and collide with the atoms of the conductor, they transfer kinetic energy into thermal energy , making the conductor warm.
Joule”s Law of Heating:
The amount of heat ( H ) produced in a conductor is calculated using the formula:
H = I2 R t   where:
I = electric current ( in amperes )
R = Resistance of the conductor ( in ohm”s }
T = Time for which the current flows ( in seconds }

slides.title: Factors that increases Heat production:
slides.text:
Factors that increases Heat production:
Higher current ( I ); Heat increases rapidly with the squre of the current.
Higher resistance ( R ):  Materials with high resistance ( like nichrome } get much hotter than low – resistance materials ( like copper }.
Longer duration ( t ): the longer the current flows , the more total heat accumulates.
Conductor shape: Thinner and longer wires offer more resistance , generating more heat.
COMMON APPLICATIONS
Heating appliances: Devices like electric irons, room heaters , kettles , and hair dryers use high – resistance nichrome coils to convert electricity into usable heat.

slides.title: SOURCE OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY
slides.text:
SOURCE OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY
Electrical energy is a secondry energy source produced by converting primary energy sources – such as fossil fuels , nuclear reactions , and natural forces – into an electrical current via generators or photovoltaic cells. The primary sources of electrical energy are divided into non – renewable and renewable categories.
NON – RENEWABLE SOURCES
Fossil fuels : Coal , natural gas , and petroleum are burned to creat heat, which produces steam to drive turbines and generators.
Nuclear Energy : Uses the heat  generated from  splitting atomic nuclei ( Nuclear fission ) in a reactor to produce steam and turn turbines.

slides.title: RENEWABLE SOURCES:
slides.text:
RENEWABLE SOURCES:
Hydropower. Uses the kinetic energy of falling or flowing water in rivers and dams to spin water turbines.
Solar Energy: Converts sunlight directly into electricity using photovoltaic solar panels, or uses solar thermal systems to create steam.
Wind Energy: Harnesses the movement of air to turn wind turbine blades connected to generators.
Geothermal Energy: Utiliizes heat from deep inside the earth to produce steam that drives poer plant turbines.
Biomass : Burns organic materials like wood , agricultural crops , or waste to create heat and steam.

slides.text:
E M F AND P D
Electromotive  force ( E M F )  and potential difference ( P D ) are both measured in volts ( V ) , but they describe different stages of energy movement in an electric circuit.
ELECTROMOTIVE FORCE ( E M F )
Definition: The total energy supplied by a power source ( like a battery or generator ) per unit charge to move electricity around a complete circuit . Think of it as the total  “push ) or open – circuit voltage available.
Key trait: It exists even when no current is flowing ( open circuit ) . It is the cause that drives charges.
Example:
A brand – new 1.5 – volt AA alkaline battery sitting on a table has an EMF of 1.5v.

slides.title: THE PROPERTIES OF X – RAYS
slides.text:
THE PROPERTIES OF X – RAYS
X-RAYS are high – energy forms of electromagnetic radiation.
CORE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
Electromagnetic nature: They belong to the electromagnetic spectrum with short wavelength ( typically 0.01 to 10 nanometers ) and high frequencies.
Speed: They travel in a straight line at the speed of light ( 3* 10 8 m/s)in a vacuum.
No mass or charge : X-ray photons are pure energy; they carry no electrical charge or mass.
No Direction: Because they are electrically neutral, electric and magnetic fields cannot deflect or steer them.
Penetrating power: They can pass through materials that block visible light , such as wood , paper, flesh , and soft tissues’.
paragraphTexts: THE PROPERTIES OF X – RAYS
X-RAYS are high – energy forms of electromagnetic radiation.
CORE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
Electromagnetic nature: They belong to the electromagnetic spectrum with short wavelength ( typically 0.01 to 10 nanometers ) and high frequencies.
Speed: They travel in a straight line at the speed of light ( 3* 10 8 m/s)in a vacuum.
No mass or charge : X-ray photons are pure energy; they carry no electrical charge or mass.
No Direction: Because they are electrically neutral, electric and magnetic fields cannot deflect or steer them.
Penetrating power: They can pass through materials that block visible light , such as wood , paper, flesh , and soft tissues’.

slides.title: Differential Absorption: Denser  materials like bone and metal absorb or block x-rays, while soft tissues let them pass through, which creates contrast in medical images’.
slides.text:
Differential Absorption: Denser  materials like bone and metal absorb or block x-rays, while soft tissues let them pass through, which creates contrast in medical images’.
Ionization ability: They  carry enough energy to strip electrons from atoms and create ions, which can trigger chemical changes or damage living cells.
Photographic and fluorescent effects: They expose photographic and x-ray film ( turning it dark/ black where exposed) and cause certain crystals to fluoresce ( emit visible light ).
Refraction and reflection: They have extremely small wavelengths, making them difficult to reflect or refract the way visible light does ( though they can undergo diffraction and scattering ).

slides.title: THE PRODUCTION OF X-RAYS
slides.text:
THE PRODUCTION OF X-RAYS
X-rays are produced inside an evacuated glass x-ray tube through a process where fast moving electrons are rapidly decelerated or cause atomic transitions when they strike a metal target.
THE PRODUCTION PROCESS IN AN X-RAY TUBE
The generation of  x-rays requires three main steps happening inside the tube
Electron emission ( thermionic emission ) :  An electrical current heats a tungsten filament at the negative cathode , causing it to”” boil off”” electrons and form a cloud of free electrons.

slides.title: Electron Acceleration: A high electrical voltage  ( measured in kilovolts or kvp) is applied between the cathode and the positive anode. This voltage pulls and accelerates the electrons across the vacuum toward the anode at up to half the speed of light.
slides.text:
Electron Acceleration: A high electrical voltage  ( measured in kilovolts or kvp) is applied between the cathode and the positive anode. This voltage pulls and accelerates the electrons across the vacuum toward the anode at up to half the speed of light.
Sudden deceleration ( Target impact ) : When the high – speed electrons crash into a heavy metal target ( usually tungsten ) on the anode, roughly 99% of their energy converts into heat while about 1% converts into x-ray photons.
TWO MECHANISMS OF X-RAY GENERATION
When electrons hit the target , x-rays are emitted through two distinct physical interactions.

slides.title: BREMSSTRAHLUNG ( BRAKING RADIATION ):
slides.text:
BREMSSTRAHLUNG ( BRAKING RADIATION ):
An incoming high-speed electron passes close to the nucleus of a tungsten atom.
The strong positive pull of the nucleus sharply bends and slows down ( brakes ) the electron.
The lost kinetic energy is released as an x-ray photon. This produces a continuous range of x-ray energies and accounts for the majority of x-rays generated’

slides.title: CHARACTERISTIC RADIATION
slides.text:
CHARACTERISTIC RADIATION
An incoming electron collides directly with an inner-shell ( eg k-shell ) electron of a target atom and knocks it out of orbit.
An electron from outer , higher –energy shell drops down to fill the empty space .
This drop releases a burst of energy in the form of  an x-ray photon with a specific , sharp energy level unique to the target material  .

slides.text:
Ossification of the clavicle
First bone to ossify in the body at 5th and 6th week intrauterine life
Begins with intramembranous ossification and ends with endochondral or cartilaginous ossification
Two primary centres at medial and lateral ends
Secondary ossification appears at the sternal end at 18th and 25th year of life and is complete by 25th and 31styr
Thus, it is also last of epiphysis of long bones to fuse
Clinicals
Commonly fractured in children
Greenstick fractures
Common site of fracture is junction of lateral and medial thirds

slides.title: The Shoulder region – Shoulder joint
slides.text:
The Shoulder region – Shoulder joint
Joint support
Several ligaments and muscles provide strength and support for the shoulder joint
Rotator cuff muscles (SITS) provide tone
A loose fibrous articular capsule covers the joint leaving 2 openings:
Between greater and lesser tubercle for passage of tendon of long head of biceps brachii
Inferior to coracoid process allowing for communication between subscapular bursa and the synovial cavity
Shunt muscles prevent dislocation:
coracobrachialis, short head of biceps, long head of triceps which assist deltoid in preventing inferior displacement
Ligaments strengthen the articular capsule:
Glenohumeral ligament
Coracohumeral ligament
Transverse humeral ligament (bridges the intertubercular sulcus converting it a canal that holds the synovial sheath and biceps brachii tendon)
Coracoacromial arch prevents superior displacement

slides.title: Forearm- Anterior compartment
slides.text:
Forearm- Anterior compartment
Also termed flexor-pronator compartment
Contains the flexor muscles with origin from the common flexor origin (the medial epicondyle of the humerus)
They are responsible for the pronation of the forearm, hence the name
These muscles on exit into the hand are held in place at the wrist by the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) and palmar carpal ligament
Ligaments are the thickenings of the antebrachial fascia
The muscles are divided into 3 layers
A superficial layer: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, and flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)
An intermediate layer or group, consisting of one muscle: flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)
A deep layer or group of three muscles: flexor digitorum profundus (FDP), flexor pollicis longus (FPL), and pronator quadratus

slides.title: Forearm- Anterior compartment
slides.text:
Forearm- Anterior compartment
The five superficial and intermediate muscles cross the elbow joint but the three deep muscles do not
Functionally, the brachioradialis is a flexor of the forearm, but it is located in the extensor (posterior) compartment and is thus supplied by the radial nerve
Therefore, the brachioradialis is a major exception to the generalization that the radial nerve supplies only extensor muscles and that all flexors lie in the anterior compartment
The long flexors of the digits (FDS and FDP) also flex the metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints
Innervation
Median nerve supplies medial 3 1/2
Ulnar nerve supplies lateral 1 1/2

slides.title: Forearm- Posterior compartment
slides.text:
Forearm- Posterior compartment
Also termed extensor-supinator compartment
Contains the extensor group of muscles responsible for the supination of the forearm
These muscles are divided into 3 groups based on their action or function
They originate from their common extensor origin (lateral epicondyle of the humerus)
All supplied by the radial nerve
Muscles that extend and abduct or adduct the hand at the wrist joint:
extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris
Muscles that extend the medial four digits:
extensor digitorum, extensor indicis, and extensor digiti minimi
Muscles that extend or abduct the thumb:
abductor pollicis longus (APL), extensor pollicis brevis (EPB), and extensor pollicis longus (EPL)

slides.title: Forearm- clinicals
slides.text:
Forearm- clinicals
Carpal tunnel syndrome
The tunnel is formed btw the carpal bones (pisiform and hamate medially as well as scaphoid and trapezoid laterally)
Carpal bones are overlaid by the flexor retinaculum which converts it into a tunnel
Flexor tendons run under (FDP) and above it (FDS)
Compression of the median nerve within this tunnel following trauma leads to median nerve palsy
Forearm – Blood supply
The brachial artery ends in the distal part of the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius by dividing into the ulnar and radial arteries, the main arteries of the forearm
The ulnar artery descends through the anterior (flexor-pronator) compartment of the forearm, deep to the pronator teres

slides.title: Forearm – Blood supply
slides.text:
Forearm – Blood supply
Pulsations of the ulnar artery can be palpated on the lateral side of the FCU tendon, where it lies anterior to the ulnar head
The ulnar nerve is on the medial side of the ulnar artery
The radial artery leaves the forearm by winding around the lateral aspect of the wrist and crossing the floor of the anatomical snuff box to reach the hand
The pulsation of the radial artery is usually measured on the distal radius between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis longus
There are superficial and deep veins in the forearm: superficial veins ascend in the subcutaneous tissue; deep veins accompany the deep arteries

slides.title: The hand
slides.text:
The hand
The hand is a musculoskeletal region
It consists of 8 carpal bones, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges, as well muscles and tendons
Muscles: extrinsic and intrinsic groups
The extrinsic groups arise from both medial (flexors) and lateral (extensors) epicondyles
They cross the wrist through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum
The Intrinsic groups:
Thenar group: Form the base of the thumb (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis)
Hypothenar group: Form the base of the little finger (abductor, flexor, and opponens digiti minimi)
Midpalmar group: Includes the lumbricals and interossei (dorsal and palmar)

Apply protection

Flex other fingers

slides.title: THUMB
slides.text:
THUMB
Projections
PA or AP and Lateral
Patient’s Positioning for PA Thumb
Seat patient alongside the X-ray couch
Extend arm, wrist and forearm
Place medial border of the hand on the film
Rotate hand medially until palmar aspect is 15 degree to film
Extend thumb and rest on a small radiolucnt pad
Avoid exerting pressure on thenar eminence
Immobilze hand with sandbag
Place anatomical marker
Collimate beam properly
Direction of Central Ray and Centring Point
DCR: Vertical
CP: Metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb
NOTE: Increase the FFD to compensate for the large OFD

slides.title: Patients’ Positioning for Lateral Hand
slides.text:
Patients’ Positioning for Lateral Hand
From the PA position, the hand is externally rotated 90 degrees
The palm of the hand is perpendicular to the cassette with the fingers extended and thumb abducted and supported parallel to the film on radio-opaqe pad
The radial and ulnar styloid processes are superimposed
DCR: Vertical
CP: Over the head of the SECOND metacarpal
Note: This projection is commonly done to identify the foreign bodies.
Patients’ Positioning for  Anteroposterior (AP) both Hands(Ball Catcher)
The patient may seat facing the table
Both forearms are supinated and placed on the table with the dorsal surface of the hands in contact with the cassette
From this position, both hands are rotated medially 45 degree into a Ball-catching position
The fingers and thumb are separated
Immobilized the lower forearms with sandbag
Place anatomical marker and collimate beam, and apply protection
DCR: Vertical
CP: A point midway between the hands at the level of the FIFTH metacarpophalangeal joint.
